topic.title: The ₹20 crore player can't have a bad day
topic.claim: The IPL auction turned fans into owners; we don't judge a player by his form anymore, we judge him by his price tag.
topic.moment: A big-ticket buy gets out for 12 off 15 balls and the comments read 'crores le liye'; an uncapped kid does the same and gets a heart emoji.

turn.believed: Fans react to how a player performs.
turn.actually: Fans react to how he performs against what he cost, because the auction made the price the first thing we learn about him.

topic.feeling: I'm angry at a player as if it was my money.
topic.villain: An auction broadcast as a show where price becomes the headline
topic.because: The auction is televised and the price sticks to a player all season. Every innings becomes a test of 'was he worth it'.
topic.payoff: Test: remember a player's last score or his auction price. Most of us remember the price.
topic.behaviour: Fans and memes mock costly players after one bad game and celebrate cheap ones for the same output.
topic.mechanism: The price is the first fact we hear, so it becomes the lens for everything after.
topic.group: Cricket fans who follow the IPL
topic.send_to: The friend who called a player 'overpriced' after his first match.
topic.why_now: Auction talk starts before every IPL season and prices become the story again.

score.why: Fans judge a player against his price tag, not his form; it's a shareable argument for any IPL group chat.

reader.point: IPL fans judge expensive players by their auction price instead of their actual performance, so the same score is treated harshly for a costly player and kindly for a cheap one.
reader.reason: The auction makes the price a TV spectacle repeated constantly, which makes fans feel like owners who are owed returns on the money.

sources.fact: Khel Now's April 2026 piece says a big IPL price tag weighs on players and affected on-field outcomes, citing Venkatesh Iyer, Pant, and young CSK buys. It also says Shreyas Iyer handled a big price well.
sources.stance: Partly supports. It backs the idea that the price tag sticks to a player and shapes how his season is judged. It doesn't mention fans, memes, or a televised auction, and it shows some costly players performing.
sources.excerpt: "the weight of a huge price tag overburdening a top player"; "the price tag was something that affected the proceedings on the ground."; "it would certainly be tough for youngsters like Kartik and Prashant to give their best with the pressure of the price tag weighing them down." (The page also says Venkatesh Iyer's average and strike rate dropped after his big contract, KKR released him before the mini-auction, Shreyas Iyer led Punjab Kings to an IPL final, and Pant did not fully justify his record price.) These lines are quoted from the fetch tool's extraction. I could not check them against the page text.

sources.fact: Onmanorama says a high IPL price tag brings huge expectations, and that costly players such as Sam Curran are scrutinised in every match.
sources.stance: Partly supports. It backs the claim that each innings is read against the price. It names franchises as the ones who rue the spend, not fans, and it says nothing about TV or memes.
sources.excerpt: "The high price tag brings along with it huge expectations"; Sam Curran "will be under the spotlight throughout IPL 2023," and his "performance in every match will be scrutinised."; Kolkata Knight Riders "expected much more from him considering the amount it spent." (Pat Cummins) These lines are quoted from the fetch tool's extraction. I could not check them against the page text.

cover.headline: In the IPL, we stopped judging players by form. We judge the [price tag].
cover.sub: Same score, two players, two very different comment sections.

paragraphs: In the IPL, we stopped judging players by their form. We judge them by their price tag.
slides.why_swipe: What does that look like in an actual match?

paragraphs: A crore-rupee buy gets out for 12 off 15. The comments: "crores le liye, aur yeh?"
An uncapped kid makes the same 12 off 15. Heart emoji. "Future star".
slides.why_swipe: Why do the same twelve runs get two opposite reactions?

paragraphs: Same twelve runs. The only difference is that we heard one player's price before we ever saw him bat.
slides.why_swipe: Where did we hear it first?

paragraphs: The auction is a TV show. Paddles go up, and the figure runs on the ticker all evening. So by the time he bats, the number has been repeated more than his name.
slides.why_swipe: And what sticks from that evening?

paragraphs: So every innings turns into an audit. Fifty off 30 from a base-price kid is a story. From the costliest buy on the team, it's "theek hai, paisa toh vasool kar."
slides.why_swipe: Is this just fans being harsh?

paragraphs: It's not cruelty. Once you know the price, every innings feels like your money is on the line.
You never paid a rupee for him. Yet his duck in the first over still feels like it came out of your salary.
slides.why_swipe: How do you know you're doing it too?

paragraphs: Name the big buy from your team. Now say his last score.
Now say his price. Under a second.

end.save: For the next auction, when the ticker starts flashing crores.
end.send: Send to the friend who called a player 'overpriced' after his first match.

draft.alt_text: A text carousel arguing that IPL fans judge players by their auction price instead of their form. It compares reactions to a costly player and an uncapped player with the same score, notes that the only difference is we heard one player's price first, explains that the televised auction makes the price the show, shows how every innings turns into an audit that feels like the fan's own money is at stake, and ends with a test: you remember a player's price faster than his last score.

claims.text: A costly buy getting out for 12 off 15 and comments reading 'crores le liye', while an uncapped player with the same output gets a heart emoji.
